primer.intro: Advanced string algorithms are built on one quiet idea: a string can partially match itself, and precomputing that self-similarity lets searches skip work instead of re-reading. The border array (also called lps, longest proper prefix which is also suffix) records, for every prefix, the longest border - a proper prefix that is simultaneously a suffix. KMP rides that array to find patterns with no backtracking. The Z-array records, for every position, how many characters from there match the string's own beginning. And rolling hashes turn any substring into a number, so two windows compare in constant time. Three tools, one theme: pay once to understand the string, then answer fast forever.
whenToUse: Finding every occurrence of a pattern in a text in linear total time.
Longest prefix of a string that is also its suffix - the border array's last entry.
Comparing many substrings for equality - rolling hashes with verification.
Periodic structure: repeats, cycles and borders are the same phenomenon.
primer.mentalModel: A border is a self-overlap: the string laid over itself, shifted, still agreeing. The lps construction grows a border by one matching character, and on a mismatch it does the only clever thing in the algorithm - it falls back to the border of the border, because any shorter self-overlap must itself be a border. That fallback chain is also why KMP runs without ever moving backwards in the text: when the pattern mismatches after matching k characters, the lps entry for k says exactly how much of the match provably survives, so the pattern slides forward and the text pointer stands still. The Z-array tells the same story from the other end - z of i is how far the string's own prefix reappears starting at i - and either array converts matching questions into table lookups.
mistakes: Resetting the matched length to zero on a mismatch - the fallback must go to lps of the previous length, or borders are lost.
Trusting equal hashes as equal strings - collisions exist; verify characters on a hash hit.
Computing the border array of the pattern alone when the trick wants pattern, separator, text joined.

example.title: The border array, grown one character at a time
example.explain: len carries the current border length. A matching character extends it; a mismatch drops len to the border of the border - the while loop - until something matches or nothing is left. Each character raises len at most once, and every fallback lowers it, so the total work is linear despite the inner loop. The final entry answers the happy-prefix question outright, and the same loop run over pattern plus separator plus text is the whole of KMP.

primer.practice: Open Practice with Reverse Every Word for a warm-up, then go straight at the LPS Array - the border array is the topic's load-bearing wall.

sections.title: The border array
sections.text: Read lps aloud for aabaaab: 0 1 0 1 2 2 3. Entry i says: the prefix ending at i has a border this long. The two ideas worth engraving: growth is one character at a time - a border of length len extends to len plus 1 exactly when the next characters agree - and shrinkage follows the chain lps of len minus 1, because any shorter self-overlap of a border is a border of the whole. Everything else in the topic is an application. Longest happy prefix: the last entry. Pattern search: build lps of pattern, separator, text, and every position where the value equals the pattern length marks an occurrence. Period of a string: length minus the last entry.

check.prompt: What is the border (lps) array of aaaa?

options.explain: Each prefix of a-runs overlaps itself one shorter: a, aa, aaa.
All zeros describes a string with no self-overlap, like abcd.
A border must be proper - the whole prefix may no more count itself.
Longer prefixes of aaaa keep longer overlaps; the values climb.

reveal.solution: For each prefix of aaaa, slide it over itself. Prefix a has no proper border: 0. Prefix aa overlaps itself by one a: 1. Prefix aaa by aa: 2. The full aaaa by aaa: 3. Hence 0 1 2 3. The first entry of any border array is 0 by definition, and a value can rise by at most 1 per step - two facts that catch most hand-calculation errors.

sections.title: Hashes and windows
sections.text: A rolling hash treats a string as digits of a number in some base, reduced by a large modulus. Its power is the slide: knowing the hash of text positions i through j, one multiply, one add and one subtract give the hash of i plus 1 through j plus 1 - so comparing a pattern against every window of the text costs constant time per window after linear setup. Rabin-Karp is exactly that loop: precompute the pattern's hash, roll a window across the text, and on every hash agreement verify the characters before reporting, because two different strings can share a hash. Choose the modulus large and the base unpredictable, and collisions become rare - but the verification step is what makes the reported positions facts rather than probabilities.

quiz.prompt: Find every occurrence of a pattern in a long text with linear total work. Which tool?

options.text: KMP: the pattern's border array tells how much match survives each mismatch
options.explain: The text pointer only advances; the pattern slides by border arithmetic.

options.text: Compare the pattern at every text position
options.explain: Worst case multiplies the lengths - the aaaa-style inputs kill it.

options.text: Sort the text's characters
options.explain: Occurrence positions live in the original order; sorting erases them.

options.text: A trie of the text's characters
options.explain: A trie indexes words; single-pattern search wants borders or hashes.

quiz.prompt: Longest prefix of s that is also a suffix (shorter than s itself). Where is the answer?

options.text: The last entry of the border array of s
options.explain: That entry is literally defined as this length.

options.text: The first entry of the border array
options.explain: The first entry is always 0 - a one-letter prefix has no proper border.

options.text: The maximum entry anywhere in the array
options.explain: Interior entries describe interior prefixes; the question is about all of s.

options.text: The count of nonzero entries
options.explain: Counting measures how many prefixes have borders, a different statistic.

quiz.prompt: Millions of substring-equality checks on one string. What setup makes each check cheap?

options.text: Prefix hashes with a rolling base - any substring's hash in O(1), verify on hits
options.explain: Equality becomes number comparison; verification guards against collisions.

options.text: Compare character by character each time
options.explain: Each check costs the substring length - the bill the hashes delete.

options.text: A border array per query
options.explain: Borders describe self-overlap of one string, pairwise equality wants hashes.

options.text: Store all substrings in a set
options.explain: Quadratically many substrings exist; materialising them is the memory wall.

quiz.prompt: What does z[i] of the Z-array promise about the string s?

options.text: s starting at i matches its own beginning for exactly z[i] characters
options.explain: Each entry measures how far the prefix reappears at position i.

options.text: The suffix at i is a palindrome of length z[i]
options.explain: Palindromes face backwards; Z compares against the prefix, forwards.

options.text: Character i repeats z[i] times
options.explain: Entries measure prefix-overlap length, nothing about single characters.

options.text: i is a period of the string when z[i] is zero
options.explain: Periods come from borders; a zero only says the prefix is absent here.
The fallback at position 5 drops from aab to a, then extends - entry 2.
Position 5 holds a, but s[2] is b - the border must shrink before growing.
All zeros is for strings with no self-overlap at all; aab overlaps a.
The mismatch falls back to the border of the border - 1, then extends to 2.

quiz.prompt: Count-and-say starts at 1. What is the 5th term?

options.explain: 1211 reads as one 1, one 2, two 1s.
1211 is the 4th term; reading it aloud gives the 5th.
312211 is the 6th term - one step too far.
Dropping the leading count breaks the read-aloud rule.

quiz.prompt: Z-array of aaab (with z[0] = 0 by convention)?

options.explain: From position 1 the prefix matches aa; from 2 just a; b matches nothing.
Position 1 reads aab against the prefix aaa - the third character disagrees.
Position 1 matches two characters, aa, before hitting the b.
The convention zeroes the first entry; the whole string is no proper overlap.

quiz.prompt: Why is the border-array construction linear despite its inner while loop?

options.text: len rises at most once per step; fallbacks only spend what the rises banked
options.explain: An amortised argument: total falls are bounded by total rises, so work is linear.

options.text: The while loop runs a constant number of times
options.explain: A single position can fall many times - it is the total that is bounded.

options.text: The array is small
options.explain: The array is length n; size is no argument about time.

options.text: It is actually n log n
options.explain: The amortised count is genuinely linear - no log appears.

quiz.prompt: Naive pattern search - compare at every position. The worst case for text n, pattern m?

options.text: About n times m, hit by inputs like aaaa text and aaab pattern
options.explain: Every position matches m-1 characters before failing at the last.

options.text: n plus m always
options.explain: Linear is KMP's promise; the naive loop re-reads matched text.

options.text: n log m
options.explain: No halving happens anywhere in the naive loop.

options.text: m squared
options.explain: The text length drives the outer loop; m alone understates it.

quiz.prompt: This lps builder returns 0 1 0 1 2 1 2 for aabaaab (truth: 0 1 0 1 2 2 3). What is the bug?

options.text: The mismatch resets len to 0 - it must fall back to lps[len - 1] and retry
options.explain: Borders nest; the border of the border often still extends, and zeroing discards it.

options.text: The loop must start at 0
options.explain: lps[0] is 0 by definition; starting at 1 is standard.

options.text: len should start at 1
options.explain: An empty border is the honest start.

options.text: The comparison is reversed
options.explain: s[i] against s[len] is exactly the extend test.

quiz.prompt: This Rabin-Karp reports an occurrence where the text differs from the pattern. What is the bug?

options.text: Equal hashes are evidence - compare the characters before reporting
options.explain: Collisions are rare, real and adversarial; verify on every hash hit.

options.text: The hash function is broken
options.explain: Any modulus hash collides somewhere; the missing verification is the flaw.

options.text: i is off by one
options.explain: The position may be fine - the phantom match is the reported lie.

options.text: push is the issue; use unshift
options.explain: Result order is cosmetic; truth of the entries is the point.

quiz.prompt: Which input most deserves a dedicated test for any pattern-search routine?

options.text: A pattern longer than the text
options.explain: The loop bounds go negative unless guarded - report no occurrences, cleanly.

options.text: A pattern of length one
options.explain: Simple and common - the degenerate long pattern breaks loops first.

options.text: Text and pattern identical
options.explain: One clean occurrence at zero; nothing boundary-shaped.

options.text: A pattern with mixed case
options.explain: Alphabet questions are policy, the length inversion is arithmetic.
